body:
Why earthquakes are geographically concentrated

Earthquakes do not occur uniformly across the Earth's surface. They are concentrated in relatively narrow belts corresponding mainly to tectonic plate boundaries, where rocks experience continuous compression, extension or shearing.

Earthquakes at plate boundaries

BoundaryPlate movementEarthquake characteristics
DivergentPlates move apartMostly shallow
Convergent with subductionOne plate descends beneath anotherShallow, intermediate and deep
Continental collisionContinents convergePredominantly shallow crustal earthquakes
TransformPlates slide past each otherMostly shallow

Major seismic belts of the world

Circum-Pacific belt

The Circum-Pacific belt, commonly called the Pacific Ring of Fire, surrounds much of the Pacific Ocean. It is characterised by frequent earthquakes, ocean trenches, subduction zones and numerous volcanoes.

Important regions include Japan, the Philippines, parts of Indonesia, New Zealand, Alaska and the western margins of North and South America. Subduction zones within this belt can generate extremely powerful earthquakes and tsunamis.

Mediterranean–Himalayan belt

Also called the Alpine–Himalayan belt, this seismic region extends broadly from the Mediterranean region through Turkey, Iran and the Himalayan region towards Southeast Asia. It reflects the convergence of several tectonic plates.

The Himalayas experience frequent earthquakes because the Indian Plate continues to converge with the Eurasian Plate. Continental collision generates strong compression and faulting.

Mid-ocean ridge belt

Earthquakes occur along divergent boundaries such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where plates separate and new oceanic crust forms. These earthquakes are generally shallow. Transform faults associated with oceanic ridges also generate seismic activity.

Earthquake-prone regions of India

India's seismic activity reflects both active plate boundaries and geological weaknesses within the Indian Plate. Important earthquake-prone regions include:

  • The Himalayan region, including Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
  • Northeastern India, including Assam and adjoining areas.
  • The Andaman and Nicobar Islands, associated with an active subduction system.
  • The Kachchh region of Gujarat, where ancient faults can be reactivated.

Peninsular India is comparatively stable, but it is not earthquake-free. The 1993 Latur earthquake in Maharashtra and the 2001 Bhuj earthquake illustrate the occurrence of damaging intraplate earthquakes.

Seismic zones of India

Seismic zoning classifies geographical areas according to their expected seismic hazard and provides a basis for earthquake-resistant structural design.

Seismic zoneRelative hazard
Zone IILow
Zone IIIModerate
Zone IVHigh
Zone VVery high

Status of India's seismic zoning standard

The Ministry of Earth Sciences stated in its parliamentary reply of 1 April 2026 that the seismic zoning map under IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 remained applicable following the withdrawal of the revised 2025 zoning notification in March 2026. Under the applicable 2016 classification, India has 4 seismic zones, from Zone II to Zone V. Zone V represents the highest hazard category. This is the verified official status used at the content cutoff of 27 November 2026.

Seismic zones represent expected regional hazard, not the magnitude of a particular earthquake. Even a low-hazard zone can experience damaging shaking under unfavourable local conditions.

Gujarat and the Kachchh seismic region

Kachchh is a highly significant intraplate seismic region containing geological faults that can be reactivated by stresses transmitted through the Indian Plate. Parts of Kachchh fall within the highest seismic hazard zone under the 2016 classification.

  • 1819 Kachchh earthquake: Associated with ground deformation and the formation of the uplifted feature known as the Allah Bund.
  • 1956 Anjar earthquake: An important historical earthquake in Kachchh.
  • 2001 Bhuj earthquake: Occurred on 26 January 2001. The US Geological Survey catalogue reports a magnitude of 7.7. Other catalogues may report different estimates.

Gujarat's earthquake risk extends beyond Kachchh. Seismic hazard, the concentration of population and infrastructure, and the vulnerability of buildings must all be considered when assessing disaster risk.

Prelims focus

  • The Circum-Pacific belt is associated with major subduction zones.
  • Mid-ocean ridge earthquakes are generally shallow.
  • The Himalayan seismic belt results largely from continental convergence.
  • Zone V is the highest hazard category under India's applicable 2016 classification.
  • The Allah Bund is associated with the 1819 Kachchh earthquake.
  • Trap: Major earthquakes can occur away from plate boundaries.

[References: NOAA JetStream, Plate Tectonics and Earthquakes; US Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Earthquake; Institute of Seismological Research, A Review of Seismic Hazard Assessment of Gujarat: A Highly Active Intra-Plate Region; US Geological Survey earthquake catalogue, event usp000a8ds, 26 January 2001; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Press Information Bureau, Parliament Question: Seismograph Network, 1 April 2026. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Global Earthquake Belts and Seismic Activity in India and Gujarat

body:
Primary and secondary earthquake hazards

Earthquakes can damage settlements and infrastructure through direct ground movement as well as through processes triggered by that movement. The scale of damage depends not only on earthquake magnitude but also on exposure and vulnerability.

Direct effects

  • Ground shaking: Vibrations may damage or collapse buildings, bridges and other structures.
  • Surface rupture: Fault displacement may break the ground and damage roads, pipelines and foundations.
  • Ground deformation: Land may rise, subside or undergo horizontal displacement.

Secondary effects

  • Landslides and rockfalls on unstable slopes.
  • Soil liquefaction and foundation failure.
  • Fires caused by damaged electrical installations or fuel lines.
  • Flooding associated with damage to dams or embankments.
  • Tsunamis generated by suitable undersea disturbances.

Soil liquefaction

Liquefaction is the temporary loss of strength and stiffness of susceptible water-saturated soil during strong shaking, causing the soil to behave more like a liquid than a stable solid.

Liquefaction occurs particularly in loose, water-saturated granular sediments such as sand and certain silty soils. Under ordinary conditions, contact between soil grains allows the soil to support loads. During strong earthquake shaking, the grains tend to rearrange, increasing pressure in the water occupying the spaces between them.

If the water cannot drain sufficiently quickly, the increased pore-water pressure reduces the effective contact between the grains. The soil may consequently lose much of its ability to support buildings and other structures.

Consequences of liquefaction

  • Buildings may sink, tilt or experience uneven settlement.
  • Buried tanks and pipes may rise towards the surface.
  • Water and sand may emerge through ground fissures, forming sand boils.
  • Ground may move laterally towards nearby riverbanks, shorelines or other free surfaces.

Liquefaction does not require soil particles to melt. It is a mechanical loss of soil strength. Loose saturated deposits in coastal plains, river valleys and reclaimed land may be particularly susceptible.

Ground fissures, sand ejection and liquefaction were documented during the 2001 Kachchh earthquake.

Hazard, exposure and vulnerability

Hazard refers to the potentially damaging physical event. Exposure refers to people, buildings and infrastructure located in the affected area. Vulnerability refers to their susceptibility to damage.

Disaster risk can be reduced even when the underlying tectonic hazard cannot be eliminated. Earthquake-resistant buildings, appropriate land use and emergency preparedness reduce vulnerability and exposure.

Earthquake risk reduction

  • Seismic zoning and microzonation: Identify regional hazard and local variations in expected shaking or ground failure.
  • Earthquake-resistant construction: Follow appropriate structural design standards and provide adequate strength and ductility, allowing structures to deform without sudden collapse.
  • Retrofitting: Strengthen vulnerable existing buildings, especially schools, hospitals and essential public facilities.
  • Land-use planning: Account for active faults, unstable slopes, liquefaction-prone ground and other local hazards.
  • Preparedness: Conduct drills, secure heavy furniture and prepare emergency communication and response arrangements.

Protective action during shaking

Indoors, the recommended general action is Drop, Cover and Hold On. Protect the head and neck, take shelter under sturdy furniture where available, and hold on until the shaking stops. Avoid windows, falling objects and lifts. Do not rush outside while severe shaking continues.

People already outdoors should move away from buildings, poles and overhead wires where possible. After the earthquake, remain alert for aftershocks and follow instructions issued by disaster management authorities.

Prelims focus

  • Loose water-saturated granular soil is particularly susceptible to liquefaction.
  • Liquefaction involves increased pore-water pressure and reduced soil strength.
  • Sand boils and lateral spreading may indicate liquefaction.
  • Retrofitting strengthens existing vulnerable structures.
  • Drop, Cover and Hold On is a standard protective action during shaking.
  • Trap: Liquefaction is not the melting of soil.

[References: NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 15, Some Natural Phenomena, Earthquakes and Protection against Earthquakes; US Geological Survey, What Are the Effects of Earthquakes?; Geological Society of India, Journal, 2001, Vol. 58, Issue 3, pp. 193–202; National Disaster Management Authority, Simplified Guidelines for Earthquake Safety of Buildings; US Geological Survey, ShakeAlert Steps. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Monitoring earthquake activity

Seismic monitoring involves the continuous recording and analysis of ground vibrations using networks of instruments. Information from multiple seismic stations helps determine the location, origin time, depth and magnitude of earthquakes.

Monitoring also helps identify active seismic regions, understand aftershock sequences and improve knowledge of geological faults. These observations provide valuable information for seismic hazard assessment and emergency response.

Prediction, forecasting and early warning

These terms describe different capabilities and should not be used interchangeably.

TermMeaning
PredictionSpecifying the time, location and magnitude of a future earthquake.
ForecastingEstimating the probability of earthquake occurrence within a region and time period.
Early warningDetecting an earthquake that has already begun and issuing an alert before strong shaking reaches some locations.

Scientists cannot reliably predict the precise time, location and magnitude of future earthquakes. Unusual animal behaviour, small preliminary earthquakes and other suggested indicators are not dependable methods of exact earthquake prediction.

How earthquake early warning works

Earthquake early warning systems take advantage of differences in seismic wave speeds and the rapid electronic transmission of information.

  1. An earthquake begins and releases seismic waves.
  2. Nearby seismic instruments detect the initial ground motion, including the faster P-waves.
  3. Automatic systems rapidly estimate the earthquake's source and expected shaking.
  4. Alerts are transmitted to locations where damaging shaking has not yet arrived.
  5. People and automated systems take protective action.

Depending on the distance from the earthquake and the speed of detection, warning may provide only a few seconds or occasionally a longer interval. Locations very close to the rupture may receive little or no useful warning.

Earthquake early warning is not earthquake prediction. It begins only after the earthquake has started.

Foreshocks and aftershocks

  • Foreshock: An earthquake preceding a larger earthquake in the same general region. It can normally be identified with confidence as a foreshock only after the larger event occurs.
  • Mainshock: The largest earthquake in an identified earthquake sequence.
  • Aftershock: An earthquake occurring after the mainshock as stresses are redistributed and rocks adjust around the affected region.

Aftershocks may continue for days, months or longer following a major earthquake. They are particularly dangerous when buildings have already been weakened by the mainshock.

Institutions relevant to India and Gujarat

  • National Centre for Seismology: An institution under the Ministry of Earth Sciences responsible for national earthquake monitoring and the dissemination of earthquake information. Its headquarters is in New Delhi.
  • Institute of Seismological Research: Located in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. It undertakes earthquake research, seismic monitoring and seismic hazard assessment, with particular relevance to Gujarat.
  • Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority: Undertakes and coordinates disaster management activities, including earthquake preparedness, mitigation and capacity building in Gujarat.
  • Bureau of Indian Standards: Formulates technical standards, including criteria for earthquake-resistant structural design.

Earthquake monitoring and earthquake-resistant construction serve complementary purposes. Monitoring provides information about seismic events and hazards, while structural measures reduce the damage that future earthquakes may cause.

Prelims focus

  • Exact earthquake prediction is not scientifically reliable.
  • Earthquake forecasting expresses probabilities.
  • Early warning operates after rupture begins.
  • The National Centre for Seismology functions under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
  • The Institute of Seismological Research is located in Gandhinagar.
  • Trap: Every earthquake is not necessarily preceded by a recognisable foreshock.

[References: NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018–19 reprint, Chapter 15, Earthquakes; US Geological Survey, Can You Predict Earthquakes?, Earthquake Early Warning Overview and ShakeAlert Steps; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Press Information Bureau, Parliament Question: Seismograph Network, 1 April 2026; Institute of Seismological Research, Gandhinagar; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
